title: Integer division
explanation: Both operands are ints, so `/` truncates: 9/4 = 2. The remainder 9%4 = 1. 2 + 1 = 3.

title: Predict the output: negative remainders
prompt: Predict exactly what each line prints.
explanation: Java's `%` takes the sign of the LEFT operand: `-7 % 3 == -1` and `7 % -3 == 1`. `Math.floorMod(-7, 3)` rounds the quotient down instead, giving `2`. Adding `b` then taking `% b` again lifts a negative remainder into `[0, b)` by hand.

title: Drill: wrap an index
prompt: From memory: a circular array has `n` slots (n ≥ 1). Return where index `i` lands after wrapping — always in `[0, n)`, even when `i` is negative. E.g. `i = -1, n = 5` → `4`.

solution.explanation: `Math.floorMod` always returns a result in `[0, n)` for positive `n`, unlike `%`, which returns negatives for negative `i`. `((i % n) + n) % n` is the equivalent by-hand form. O(1).

hints: Plain `%` is right for positive `i` but gives a negative answer for negative `i`.
Java has a `Math` method designed for exactly this — or fix the sign by adding `n` and taking the remainder again.

title: Short-circuit order
prompt: `d` might be `0`. Which condition is safe?
options: `n / d > 1 && d != 0` — same thing, order doesn't matter
explanation: `&&` evaluates left to right and stops at the first false. Checking `d != 0` first means `n / d` is never computed when `d` is zero. The reversed order divides first and throws `ArithmeticException: / by zero`. Later, the same rule makes `i < arr.length && arr[i] > 0` safe.

title: Math toolbox
code:
int bigger = Math.{{1}}(a, b);          // larger of the two
int distance = Math.{{2}}(a - b);       // always non-negative
int pow = (int) Math.{{3}}(2, 10);      // 1024 — note the cast
explanation: `Math.pow` returns `double` even for whole numbers, hence the `(int)` cast.

title: Predict the output: bit operators
prompt: Predict exactly what each line prints. (6 is `110` in binary, 3 is `011`.)
explanation: `5 & 1` keeps only the lowest bit → 1 (odd). `110 ^ 011 = 101` → 5. `1 << 4` = 2^4 = 16. `>>` copies the sign bit, so -8 >> 1 = -4. `-1` is 32 one-bits; `>>> 28` shifts in zeros, leaving the top 4 ones at the bottom: `1111` = 15.

title: Drill: odd one out with XOR
prompt: From memory: among `a`, `b`, `c`, two values are equal and one may differ. Return the value that doesn't have a partner (if all three are equal, return that value). Use `^` — no `if` needed.

solution.explanation: XOR is commutative and `x ^ x == 0`, `x ^ 0 == x`. The equal pair cancels to 0, leaving the unpaired value. The same idea over a whole array solves Single Number in O(n) time, O(1) space.

hints: XOR has two key facts: a value XORed with itself is 0, and XOR with 0 changes nothing.
Order doesn't matter for XOR, so combining all three lets the equal pair cancel.

title: Sum of digits
prompt: Return the sum of the digits of `n` (n ≥ 0). Peel digits with `% 10` and `/ 10` in a loop: while `n > 0`, add `n % 10` to a running total, then set `n = n / 10`.

solution.explanation: `n % 10` reads the last digit; `n /= 10` removes it. The loop ends when every digit is consumed. O(number of digits).

hints: Repeat two steps until nothing is left: read the last digit, then remove it.
Loop `while (n > 0)` — `n % 10` is the last digit, `n / 10` drops it.
Inside the loop: `sum += n % 10;` then shrink `n`.

title: Drill: clamp
prompt: From memory: return `x` clamped into the range `[lo, hi]` — if `x < lo` return `lo`, if `x > hi` return `hi`, else `x`. One line with `Math.max` and `Math.min` is the idiomatic answer.

solution.explanation: `Math.min(x, hi)` caps the top; `Math.max(lo, ...)` lifts the bottom.

hints: Clamping is two separate limits: one ceiling, one floor.
`Math.min(x, hi)` enforces the ceiling — then wrap that result in a `Math.max` with `lo`.

title: Recall: Math toolbox
prompt: Fill in the three Math calls you'll use constantly.
code:
int hi = Math.{{1}}(a, b);   // larger of the two
int lo = Math.{{2}}(a, b);   // smaller of the two
int d  = Math.{{3}}(a - b);  // non-negative distance
explanation: `Math.max`, `Math.min`, and `Math.abs` — the three you reach for in almost every problem.

title: Drill: range of three
prompt: From memory: return the range (largest minus smallest) of three ints, using nested `Math.max` / `Math.min`.

solution.explanation: `Math.max`/`Math.min` take two arguments, so nest one call inside another to cover three values. Range is then max minus min.

hints: Find the largest and the smallest separately, then subtract.
Nest to get the max of three: `Math.max(a, Math.max(b, c))`.
Do the same with `Math.min`, then subtract.
